The Secret Ingredients for Perfect Tempura | Kenji Eats Japan

J. Kenji López-Alt

Aug 5, 2026
 
View in app
View in app

A modernized tempura batter with vodka and club soda delivers restaurant-quality crispness without years of apprenticeship.

What makes tempura—Japanese-style battered and fried vegetables and seafood—so unique? The key lies in the texture of the coating. Unlike more heavily-battered foods that can sometimes end up equal parts batter to food, with tempura, the coating should be lacy and whisper-thin, with plenty of bubbly nooks and crannies for adding texture and absorbing sauce. More than any other type of battering, tempura allows the flavor of the ingredients being battered to shine through.

Tempura arrived in Japan with Portuguese missionaries in the sixteenth century. The Japanese word tempura comes the Portuguese word tempora, which referred to the days in which they abstained from meat, instead cooking battered-and-fried fish.

Over the centuries Japanese cooks transformed it into something entirely its own, using lighter flours and specialized technique. Today, at the best tempura restaurants, a single chef will serve you at a counter. Seasonal vegetables, seafood, and mushrooms are served one piece at a time, each fried to order and eaten within seconds. It's one of the purest expressions of the idea that technique exists to reveal an ingredient rather than cover it up.

Fortunately, you don't need years of apprenticeship to make excellent tempura at home. You just need to understand what the ingredients in the batter are doing, and how to maximize their effects.

Starch Contrast

The defining characteristic of tempura is its extraordinary lightness. The batter should puff into a web of delicate bubbles rather than forming a thick crust. To make that happen, we're trying to solve two competing problems. We need just enough structure that the batter clings to the food, but we want as little gluten development as possible, since gluten makes batters chewy instead of crisp.

The solution is to swap out some of the wheat flour in a standard batter with a pure starch instead. The wheat flour in a standard batter provides proteins that form just enough gluten to hold everything together and enough natural sugars and proteins to develop a pale golden color as it fries. Use flour alone, however, and the crust becomes heavier and breadier than true tempura.

The starches solve that problem. Cornstarch crisps beautifully because it forms a loose, brittle network when it fries. Potato starch behaves differently. As it cooks, it forms a slightly more elastic gel before drying exceptionally crisp. Combining the two gives you a coating that's lighter than flour alone, crisper than either starch by itself, and remarkably delicate. The flour supplies the framework; the starches fill it in with crunch.

Next comes the egg. Compared to many Western batters, tempura uses surprisingly little egg—just enough to provide a little protein for structure and a touch of richness. Too much egg would brown too quickly and produce a thicker, cakier coating. Here, it acts almost like another structural ingredient rather than a flavoring.

Water We Talking About?

The liquid is where things get more interesting. Traditional tempura uses ice-cold water, and keeping it cold is critical. Cold batter slows gluten development and helps preserve the tiny air bubbles that make the coating feel so light. But we can push things even further.

Instead of water, I like to use a combination of ice-cold vodka and ice-cold club soda.

Vodka improves crispness for two reasons. First, alcohol evaporates at a lower temperature than water, so as soon as the batter hits the hot oil it flashes rapidly into vapor, creating extra bubbles inside the coating. Second, gluten does not form in alcohol, only in water. So by cutting the liquid with some vodka, we are able to create a well-hydrated batter that has proportionally less gluten development than an equivalent batter made from pure water. The result is a batter that's both lighter and more forgiving.

Club soda contributes in a different way. The dissolved carbon dioxide forms tiny bubbles throughout the batter that expand as they hit the oil, adding even more lightness. Club soda also contains a small amount of dissolved sodium, which helps it retain carbonation a little longer than plain sparkling water. And because ice-cold water holds carbonation better than warm water, it preserves those bubbles until the very last moment.

Smooth (is) Criminal

Mixing matters just as much as the ingredients.

For pancakes, muffins, or cakes, we're taught not to overmix because gluten makes them tough. Tempura follows the same principle but taken to an extreme.

Instead of whisking until everything is homogeneous, I pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir vigorously with chopsticks while shaking the bowl—mixing tempura batter is a two-handed operation. The motion quickly moistens most of the flour while leaving small pockets of dry flour scattered throughout the batter. Those dry pockets hydrate only as the food fries, creating the irregular, craggy texture that defines good tempura. If the batter looks unfinished, you're doing it right.

Even so, tempura batter has a limited lifespan. The longer it sits, the more thoroughly the flour hydrates and the more gluten develops. The bubbles from the club soda slowly escape, the starches absorb more liquid, and the batter becomes smoother, heavier, and less crisp. If you're frying for more than fifteen or twenty minutes, it's worth mixing a fresh batch. The ingredients are inexpensive, and the difference is immediately noticeable.

To fry, I heat a neutral oil to about 350°F (175°C), dip the ingredient lightly into the batter, let the excess drip away, then lower it gently into the oil. The key here is to use your fingers or chopsticks to gently lower the food into the oil, letting it go when your fingers are just above the surface. This may sound dangerous, but it minimizes the risk of hot oil splashing out if you drop the food in from too high. Hot oil senses fear.

As soon as the food enters the oil, keep it moving with chopsticks or a spider so fresh oil continually washes over its surface. This encourages faster, more even cooking and a crisper coating. Most foods cook in about a minute—just long enough for the coating to become pale blond and crisp without taking on much color.

That pale color is intentional. Unlike fried chicken or fish and chips, tempura isn't chasing deep browning. You're looking for delicacy: a whisper-thin shell that shatters when you bite into it, revealing the vegetable or seafood underneath almost unchanged and just barely-cooked.

Once you understand why each ingredient is there, tempura stops being a recipe and becomes a technique. Spring asparagus, summer squash blossoms, autumn mushrooms, winter broccoli, shrimp, white fish, even leafy greens—all of them can follow the same blueprint. The batter stays the same, only the ingredient changes with the seasons.

The recipe below will work for any seafood or vegetable. The key is to cut the vegetables or fish into thin-enough pieces that they fry through in the short time it takes to crisp the batter. For green vegetables, that means no more than a half-inch-thick or so. For heartier root vegetables like sweet potatoes or carrot, I cut them about 1/4-inch thick.

And if you want more tempura recipes inspired by this technique, join our Cookbook Club here on Patreon for three bonus recipes coming this Friday!
Recipe: Vegetable Tempura

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • The batter fries up extraordinarily light and crisp, with a delicate lacy texture that lets the vegetables remain the star.

  • Vodka and ice-cold club soda make the batter more forgiving than traditional tempura while producing an even crispier crust.

  • Once you learn the batter, you can tempura almost any quick-cooking vegetable—or shrimp, fish, or mushrooms—with equally great results.

Yield: Serves 4-6
Active Time: 30 minutes
Total Time: 30 minutes
Notes: Keep every ingredient for the batter as cold as possible until the moment you mix it. The batter should never be smooth—a few lumps are exactly what you're after. If you're frying for more than about 15 minutes, mix up a fresh batch of batter for the best texture. Tempura should be pale blond rather than deeply browned. If it's taking on much color, your oil is probably too hot or the food has been left in too long.

Ingredients

For the optional dipping sauce:

  • 1 cup (240ml) dashi

  • 3 tablespoons (45ml) mirin

  • 1 tablespoon (15ml) soy sauce

  • Grated daikon radish

For the batter:

  • 1/2 cup (65g) all-purpose flour

  • 1/4 cup (30g) cornstarch

  • 1/4 cup (35g) potato starch

  • 1 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt (or 1/2 teaspoon Morton kosher salt)

  • Small pinch MSG (optional)

  • 1 large egg

  • 1/4 cup (60ml) ice-cold vodka

  • 1/2 cup (120ml) ice-cold club soda

For frying:

  • 2 quarts (2L) peanut oil, vegetable oil, or shortening

For the vegetables, choose one or a combination of the below (about 1 pound total):

  • Sweet potato, peeled and sliced 1/4 inch thick

  • Kabocha or butternut squash, peeled and sliced 1/4 inch thick

  • Onion, cut into 1/2-inch rings

  • Green beans, trimmed

  • Bell peppers, cut into strips

  • Zucchini, sliced into rounds

  • Eggplant, sliced into rounds

  • Mushrooms (shiitake, oyster, or cremini)

  • Broccoli or cauliflower florets

  • Shungiku or other leafy greens

For serving:

  • Kosher salt

  • Lemon wedges

Method

  1. If making the dipping sauce: Combine the dashi, mirin, and soy sauce in a small saucepan and heat until just steaming. Let cool on the counter while you make your tempura. Alternatively, the sauce can also be mixed and served cold. Heating it briefly will evaporate off the hint of alcohol it gets from the mirin and sake and give it a mellower flavor. Add grated daikon just before serving.

  2. Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C) in a wok, Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Meanwhile, combine the flour, cornstarch, potato starch, salt, and MSG in a large bowl.

  3. Whisk together the egg, vodka, and club soda until homogeneous. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients. Using chopsticks, stir while shaking the bowl with your other hand until the batter is just barely combined. It should still contain visible lumps and even small pockets of dry flour. Do not overmix.

  4. Working in batches, dip the vegetables into the batter, allowing the excess to drip off. Carefully lower them into the oil, bringing your hand as close to the surface as possible before releasing them to minimize splashing.

  5. Fry, moving the vegetables gently with chopsticks or a spider so they're constantly exposed to fresh oil. Cook until the batter is pale blond and crisp, about a minute. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate or wire rack and season immediately with salt. Continue with the remaining vegetables.

  6. Serve immediately, either plain, with lemon wedges, or with the dipping sauce.
